To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neuropathological substrates of cognitive impairment and its culmination in dementia are complex, but that the major substrates are Alzheimer's disease, Lewy body disease, and vascular brain injury, and that the clinical pathology of these diseases is being revolutionized by new neuroimaging techniques.

the neuropathologic substrates of cognitive impairment and dementing illness are diverse, that they can be identified with high sensitivity and specificity by the tools of anatomic neuropathology, that the pathologic substrates can be detected in the blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and urine of living persons, and that the clinical and pathologic findings can be integrated to provide a framework for clinical investigation of cognitive impairment and its dementing sequelae.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the anatomic and clinical pathologic correlates of the dementias and with the clinical pathologic correlates and pathologic substrates of cognitive impairment.
the anatomic pathology of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias.
the anatomic pathology and clinical pathology of dementia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the tools of anatomic (and clinical) pathology have provided key contributions to our understanding of cognitive impairment and its culmination in dementia.
the tools of anatomic pathologists and clinical pathologists are essential for the study and treatment of the diseases that cause dementia in the coming generation.

the pathologist's role in the study of cognitive impairment and dementing illnesses has evolved and will continue to evolve in response to the changing needs of the clinician, the patient, and the public.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are now at a point where we can begin to understand the pathophysiology of cognitive impairment and to develop effective interventions.
anatomic pathology is providing the tools to define the disease processes that cause cognitive impairment and its culmination in dementia.
we have made progress in our understanding of the anatomic and clinical pathogenesis of dementia, and that the pathogenesis is more complex than previously thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the anatomic pathology of the brain and the clinical chemistry of blood and cerebrospinal fluid are both essential tools for the study of cognitive impairment and its culmination in dementia.
the anatomic pathology of the brain is complex and heterogeneous, and the clinical pathology of cognitive decline is complex and heterogeneous.
the pathologic substrate of dementia syndromes in older adults is complex.
